Learn React Eventually, So Why Not Now?

Why Learn React Eventually? Learn It Now! - React Router Lazy Loading (28)
Why Learn React Eventually? Learn It Now!

This post covers one of the most important optimizations in React Router: Lazy Loading. It's genuinely a big deal in real-world development. Lazy Loading lets you split your code into separate chunks and only load the file you actually need when you need it. So in this post, I'll walk through how Lazy Loading works and how to wire it up with Suspense.
You Don't Have to Read Clean Code to Write Decent Code

This post took me close to a year to write — it's a collection of real code smells I've seen in my time as a TA, anonymized and cleaned up. Not a Clean Code book recap; more like "here are common patterns that hurt readability, and how to write them so future-you (or your reviewer) doesn't suffer." Naming, var vs let/const, ES6 destructuring, comments, formatting, ternaries, loops, and not mixing Composition API with Options API.

React, Why Not Learn It Now?

Since we've been doing everything the Hook way in this series, it makes sense that React Router ships its own set of Hooks too. In this post I'll walk through the ones you'll bump into most often — useLocation, useParams, useNavigate, and useRoutes — with small examples for each so you know what they do and when to reach for them.

Nested routes show up all the time in real-world development, so this post walks through what they are, how to set them up, and why the `<Outlet />` component is the missing piece that makes shared layouts work.

For tiny projects, everything we've covered so far is honestly more than enough. But real projects don't work like that — as the app grows, your pages get more and more complex, and at some point you need a tool to help you manage them. That tool is React Router. In this post I'll introduce what it is, walk through SPA basics, and get a minimal router up and running.
